You'll build two things that belong to you rather than to the course: a PDF CV made from plain-text data files, and a one-page website made from the course starter. Both live in new repositories in your own GitHub account. Today you start both; by Thursday, October 15, both render and Amanda and I can see them.

# Your CV and website

## Why build these now?

You'll need a CV for job applications, fellowships, grants, and conferences. Starting it now gives you a place to keep track of research, teaching, and service as you do them.

A website gives potential collaborators and employers one link to your work and contact information. A working paper belongs there even before it's published, as long as you describe its status accurately.

You don't need a long publication list to start. Today we'll use your education, current work, and semester paper.

## What the CV and website each do

| CV | Website |
|---|---|
| A detailed record of education and experience | A short introduction with selected work and links |
| A PDF you can send with an application | A page you can update without sending a new attachment |
| Useful even if you keep it private | Can link to your CV PDF, if you want |

Both projects live in your own GitHub account and stay with you after the course. The CV repository is private; the website can be public or private. Today's CV and site don't go in your coursework repository.

## What Quarto and Typst do

You've rendered Typst PDFs since 01b. Quarto builds the document from your source and supporting files; **Typst** arranges the text on the PDF pages.

This CV uses the same route, with the template's extension supplying its layout.

You'll edit the Quarto, YAML, and BibTeX files, then click Render. You don't need to write Typst code today.

## A CV template supplies the layout

A Quarto template is a starter you download: an example document, supporting files, and any extension needed for its format. It gives you something that already renders, which you then adapt.

Christopher Kenny's [`quarto-cv`](https://github.com/christopherkenny/quarto-cv) (MIT license) supplies sample entries in YAML and BibTeX, plus an extension that controls the PDF layout.

Replace the sample entries with yours. The template handles the formatting, while Git records changes to your source files. The bibliography uses the BibTeX skills from 06b.

A GitHub Pages site is on the open web and search engines index it, so leave off anything you wouldn't put on a conference name badge: home address, personal phone number, student ID.

## What's a fork, and when would you use one?

A **fork** is a separate GitHub repository copied from someone else's, including its history. GitHub keeps a connection to the original, called the **upstream** repository. You can edit your fork without changing the original.

Fork when you want to adapt someone else's research code, maintain your own version of a tool, or propose a bug fix to a package. A **pull request** asks the original project's maintainers to review and incorporate your changes. I forked Christopher Kenny's CV template to prepare our course starter.

Today, choose **Use this template**, not Fork. It creates your own CV or website project from the starter files with a fresh history. Neither route automatically applies later changes from the original; bringing those changes in is a separate action. **Cloning** then downloads your repository to your computer, whether it began as a fork or from a template.

# Part 1: Your CV

## Make your own copy and open it

Go to [github.com/bshor/cv-starter](https://github.com/bshor/cv-starter), a fork of Christopher Kenny's `quarto-cv` template, and choose **Use this template → Create a new repository**. Pick your own account as owner, name it `cv`, choose **Private**, and create it.

On the new repository's page, click the green **Code** button and copy the HTTPS URL. In RStudio, choose **File → New Project → Version Control → Git** and paste the URL. Set **Create project as subdirectory of** to `~`, check **Open in new session**, and choose **Create Project**. `~` is your home folder: RStudio creates `~/cv` beside your coursework folder, not inside it. Keep your coursework window open for this workbook.

Which folder did RStudio put your `cv` project in? It's shown at the top of the CV window's Files pane: `___`

The starter has `cv.qmd`, `cv.Rproj`, `education.yaml`, `honors.yaml`, `positions.yaml`, `working_papers.bib`, three publication `.bib` files, two citation styles, and the `_extensions/cv/` layout. You edit the YAML and BibTeX files; the extension handles the layout.

## Render it once before editing

In the CV window, open `cv.qmd` from the Files pane and click **Render**. You get a sample CV for the political scientist Sidney Verba. A warning about an unknown font family is harmless.

## The author block and education.yaml

The `author:` block at the top of `cv.qmd` is the YAML list format from 06b: the hyphen starts an entry, the indented lines belong to it, and `affiliations` is a list inside that entry. Delete lines you don't want, such as `url`.

The body is mostly shortcodes. `{{{< cv education >}}}` is a placeholder that Quarto fills in from the `education` entries in `education.yaml`:

```yaml
education:
  University of Houston:
    - degree: Ph.D. student, Political Science
      year:
        start: 2025
  Rice University:
    - degree: B.A., Political Science
      year:
        end: 2021
```

Each institution name ends with a colon and holds a list of degrees. A `start` year without an `end` prints as "Present." Put the most recent first.

## Your Turn: put yourself in the CV

*~6 minutes.*

- Replace the author block with your name, UH email, department, and current title.
- Replace `education.yaml` with your own degrees, most recent first.
- Put one real honor, fellowship, or award in `honors.yaml`, or delete the Honors section for now.
- Render and check your name, degrees, and dates.

## One bibliography per section

```yaml
bibliography:
  books: "books.bib"
  bookchapters: "book_chapters.bib"
  articles: "journal_articles.bib"
  workingpapers: "working_papers.bib"
nocite: '@*'
```

Each name on the left labels one `.bib` file, and `:::{#refs-articles}` in the body lists the entries from the file labeled `articles`. In 06b, only cited sources appeared in the reference list; `nocite: '@*'` lists every entry instead, without any citations.

## Working papers, and publications if you have them

`working_papers.bib` holds a placeholder. Replace it with your semester paper, in RStudio or JabRef:

```bibtex
@unpublished{ruiz_turnout_2026,
  author = {Ruiz, Ana},
  title = {Early Voting and Turnout in Texas Counties},
  year = {2026}
}
```

`@unpublished` is the BibTeX type for a paper that isn't published yet. The `workingpapers` label and the `:::{#refs-workingpapers}` block are already connected.

If you have publications, keep `articles` (and `books` or `bookchapters` if they apply), export your papers from your Google Scholar profile with **Export → BibTeX** or import them as in 06b, and check each entry in JabRef. If you don't, delete those lines under `bibliography:` and their `:::{#refs-...}` blocks.

# Part 2: Your website

## Choose your route

| Route | Repository name | Who can see the site |
|---|---|---|
| Public | `YOURUSERNAME.github.io` | anyone, at `https://YOURUSERNAME.github.io` |
| Private | `site` | invited collaborators, viewing a local copy |

Which route are you taking, and why? `___`

## The repository name determines the URL

For the account `borisshor`:

| Repository name | Published website URL |
|---|---|
| `borisshor.github.io` | `https://borisshor.github.io/` |
| `beta-web-f26` | `https://borisshor.github.io/beta-web-f26/` |

For your main professional site, name the repository **your GitHub username plus `.github.io`**, exactly. That gives you the shorter URL without an extra repository name at the end. A beta or other project repository instead publishes at `https://YOURUSERNAME.github.io/REPOSITORY/`.

After enabling Pages, check **Settings → Pages** for the actual published URL and wait for deployment to finish. A newly enabled site can briefly return 404 even when the settings are correct.

## Create your copy and open it

Go to [github.com/bshor/cv-minimal-site](https://github.com/bshor/cv-minimal-site) and choose **Use this template → Create a new repository**. Public route: name it `YOURUSERNAME.github.io`, with your GitHub username exactly, and choose **Public**. Private route: name it `site` and choose **Private**.

Copy the new repository's HTTPS URL from the green **Code** button. In RStudio, choose **File → New Project → Version Control → Git** and paste the URL. Check these fields before creating the project:

- **Project directory name:** `YOURUSERNAME.github.io` for the public route, or `site` for the private route. For a beta repository with another name, use that actual repository name.
- **Create project as subdirectory of:** `~`.
- Check **Open in new session**, then choose **Create Project**.

This puts the website folder beside your CV and coursework folders. Use the site window for editing, rendering, and Git; keep your coursework window open for these notes. The repository name on GitHub determines the website URL; the local folder name doesn't change it.

## The site settings and the CV link

In `_quarto.yml`, `output-dir: docs` writes the finished site into `docs/`; `resources` copies `files/` into it. Keep the navbar. Choose how people will view your website:

1. **Public website:** enable GitHub Pages in the later publishing step. Anyone can see the page and any files copied into it, including the CV.
2. **Private website:** leave Pages off and invite Amanda and me. We view a downloaded copy locally. The navbar and its CV link still work in that local copy.

Including the CV is a separate choice in either route. The starter's CV menu item points to `files/cv.pdf`. To use it, copy your actual rendered PDF there using one of the routes below.

## Keep the navbar without a CV link

If you aren't including the PDF, change just the menu item's two lines in `_quarto.yml` to:

```yaml
      - text: "Home"
        href: index.qmd
```

Keep `navbar:` and `right:` above them; don't delete the whole navbar. The menu now opens your front page instead of a missing PDF. If you've already copied the PDF, delete both `files/cv.pdf` and `docs/files/cv.pdf` in the site's Files pane, then render, commit, and push. Changing the link doesn't remove files or earlier public Git history.

On a public site, a linked CV is public too. What did you choose, and why? `___`

## Copy the PDF through the Files pane

Skip copying if you aren't linking your CV. Otherwise, choose this GUI route **or** the Terminal route below; you only need to copy once.

1. In the **CV window's Files pane**, locate the rendered PDF and check the box beside it. Don't select the QMD source.
2. Choose **More → Copy To**. In the folder dialog, navigate to your website project folder and open its `files` folder. Confirm the copy. If both projects are siblings, go up to their parent folder, then into the website folder and `files`.
3. Return to the **site window's Files pane** and open `files`. Confirm the PDF appears. If it has another name, check its box, click **Rename**, and name the copy `cv.pdf`, matching the site's link.
4. Render the website, check its CV link in the browser, then commit and push the site changes.

Use **Copy**, not Move: keep the original PDF in the CV project. Repeat the copy after updating your CV. This works within RStudio Desktop or RStudio Server; you don't need Finder or File Explorer.

## Find and copy your CV PDF

Skip this step if you aren't linking your CV. Otherwise, in the **site window's Terminal**, run:

```bash
ls -l ..
```

`ls` lists files and folders; `-l` shows details; `..` means the parent folder. Read the names at the end of the lines. Find the CV folder you created earlier; use its actual name, not necessarily `cv`. For example, Boris's is `fall26-6394`.

Replace `CV_FOLDER` below with that name and run:

```bash
ls -l "../CV_FOLDER"
```

This lists the files inside your CV folder. Find the rendered PDF. Then copy it:

```bash
cp "../CV_FOLDER/cv.pdf" files/cv.pdf
```

`cp` copies a file. The first path is the source: replace `CV_FOLDER` and, if necessary, `cv.pdf` with your actual folder and PDF names. Keep the destination `files/cv.pdf` unchanged because the site's link expects that name. Quotes allow spaces in the source path. For example, if the folder is `fall26-6394` and the PDF is `cv.pdf`, run `cp "../fall26-6394/cv.pdf" files/cv.pdf`.

If your CV folder isn't listed, check the location you recorded in the CV step; don't guess. Confirm `cv.pdf` appears in the site's `files/` folder. Copy the PDF again whenever your CV changes, then render the website before committing and pushing.

- Write two or three sentences under About.

## Render, commit, and push

In the site window's **Build** pane, click **Render Website**. It renders the whole site into `docs/`. Open `docs/index.html` from the Files pane with **View in Web Browser**. Then, in the Git pane, stage everything, including `docs/`, commit with a message such as `Personalize my site`, and push. Commit `docs/` too: here it's the published site, not throwaway output.

Rendering only creates `docs/` on your computer. The website won't appear online until you commit and push the entire folder, including `docs/index.html`. After pushing, open the repository on GitHub and confirm that `docs/index.html` is there. If the website returns 404, check the latest deployment under **Actions**; enabling Pages alone doesn't upload your rendered files.

**Predict:** you edit `index.qmd`, commit, and push, but forget to click **Render Website** first. What does the public site show? `___`

## Public or private: finish the route

- **Public:** on GitHub, **Settings → Pages**, set Source to *Deploy from a branch* and Branch to `main`, folder `/docs`, then **Save**. Wait for deployment to finish and open the URL shown there; its form depends on the repository name, as explained above.
- **Private:** keep the repository private. Under **Settings → Collaborators → Add people**, invite `bshor` and `ataustin06`, then send us the repository's URL. Don't enable Pages: this route has no hosted URL, and a private repository doesn't make a Pages website private.

## Check the deployment in Actions

For a public site, open the website repository's **Actions** tab after enabling Pages or pushing an update. Click the newest **pages build and deployment** run. Yellow means queued or running; a green check means deployment succeeded; a red X means it failed. Click a failed job to read its error.

Check the run's time and commit: an old red run doesn't describe your latest push. If no new run appears, confirm your push succeeded. If the error says `docs/` is missing, check that `docs/index.html` reached GitHub, then commit and push the complete folder if needed. Once the deployment succeeds, open the link in **Settings → Pages**.

## Private route: open the page locally

In the site's RStudio window, open **Files → docs**, click `index.html`, and choose **View in Web Browser**. Check the picture and links. Clicking the HTML file on GitHub shows source code rather than the finished page.
